    Fifty Rule-Defined Trading Strategies for Rainbow Trader

    Scope and notation

    This catalog is intentionally strategy-first. It assumes a strong Rainbow rule engine with arithmetic, rolling-window functions, cross and signal features, higher-timeframe and context-symbol features, regime features, and a bot-side rules layer that can open, add, reduce, close, reverse, and edit stops or targets. I am not treating the current simple rule_based implementation as the final boundary here. I also am not pretending I verified private Rainbow feature keys in this run, so every feature name below is pseudocode that should be mapped onto your canonical Rainbow feature names. The point of this report is to give you 50 concrete strategies and, from them, expose exactly which rule primitives and bot actions matter most.

    I will use the following shorthand:

    • x{-1} = latest fully closed slot for feature x
    • x{-n:-1} = rolling window from -n to -1
    • cross_up(a,b) = a{-2} <= b{-2} and a{-1} > b{-1}
    • cross_down(a,b) = inverse
    • highest(high{-20:-1}), lowest(low{-20:-1}), avg(...), zscore(...), count(...), bars_since(...)
    • htf_* = higher-timeframe feature
    • ctx_* = context-symbol or market-wide feature
    • regime_* = precomputed trend/range/volatility/risk regime feature
    • signal_* = precomputed signal feature if you decide to expose signals as features too

    The evidence base behind the stronger families in this catalog is real. Time-series momentum and long-horizon trend following have a deep academic and practitioner record across futures and broader markets; dual momentum and cross-sectional momentum also have strong literature; pairs/stat-arb has a mature literature; Donchian channels, Bollinger Bands, and VWAP are canonical building blocks in deployed trading systems. citeturn0search3turn4search1turn4search5turn4search6turn4search10turn4search11turn4search0turn5search0turn6search15turn5search5

    Model-rule and bot-rule templates

    A good way to structure these strategies is exactly the split you described: a model rule emits LONG, SHORT, or NONE, and a bot rule decides whether to actually enter, how to manage the position, and how to exit. That is also close to how mature systems talk about strategies: TradingView strategies model entries, exits, multi-level exits, and trailing orders; LEAN exposes rolling windows and order tickets that can be updated or canceled; MQL5 explicitly models trailing-stop and reverse logic; Backtrader has signal-driven auto-operation plus stop and stop-trail patterns. citeturn3search5turn3search4turn3search8turn3search2turn3search6turn3search3

    To keep the 50 strategies readable, I define eight reusable bot profiles. Each strategy below references one of these profiles.

    Bot profiles

    Profile Use case Bot entry logic Bot management and exit logic
    TR Trend rider If model_signal == LONG/SHORT, risk_ok, spread_ok, liquidity_ok, open at base size. Initial stop at 2*atr_14; move to break-even at +1R; optional add on fresh continuation breakout with additions < 2; exit on opposite model signal, chandelier stop, or hard stop.
    BO Breakout follow-through Enter only if breakout closes outside trigger level and optional persistence or retest passes. Hard stop just inside broken range; if no follow-through of at least 0.5*ATR in N bars, close; partial at 1.5R; trail rest by 2.5*ATR.
    PB Pullback continuation Enter on signal only if pullback depth and trend filters hold. Stop beyond pullback low/high or 1.5*ATR; no chase if price is already extended; exit on trend invalidation, opposite signal, or 2R + trail.
    MR Mean reversion Enter only after an extreme begins reverting, not on the first touch alone. Small stop beyond extreme or 1*ATR; partial at mean or mid-band; full exit at opposite band/neutral oscillator; no pyramiding.
    IN Intraday VWAP/session logic Enter only within allowed session window and with session liquidity filter. Flatten at session end; stop at session VWAP or intraday structure; no overnight carry unless explicitly enabled.
    FR Failure reversal Enter after breakout failure, trap, or exhaustion confirmation. Stop beyond failure wick/extreme; first target at VWAP or range mid; second target at opposite side of range; fast time-stop if reversal stalls.
    SP Spread or pairs mean reversion Open synchronized long-short legs if supported. Exit when spread z-score reverts to 0 or partial at 0.5; stop if spread expands to catastrophic bound; idle if only one leg can execute.
    HY Regime-switch hybrid Use TR if trend regime, MR if range regime. Management profile switches with regime; if regime flips against the open trade, reduce or close according to policy.

    Fifty strategy definitions

    Trend and breakout systems

    Trend following and breakout strategies are the most evidence-backed part of classic systematic trading. The strongest academic base here is time-series momentum and trend following, while Donchian/Turtle-style channel breakouts are one of the oldest operational forms of that logic. citeturn0search3turn4search1turn4search5turn6search6turn6search15

    ID Strategy Evidence Model rule pseudocode Bot profile Fit Primitive stress
    1 EMA fast/slow crossover B LONG if cross_up(ema_20, ema_50) and adx_14{-1} > 20; SHORT if cross_down(...) and adx_14{-1} > 20; else NONE TR Native X, W
    2 SMA 50/200 regime cross B LONG if cross_up(sma_50, sma_200); SHORT if cross_down(sma_50, sma_200); else NONE TR Native X
    3 Triple EMA alignment B LONG if ema_10{-1} > ema_20{-1} > ema_50{-1} and slope(ema_50{-10:-1}) > 0 and close{-1} > ema_10{-1}; SHORT inverse TR Native W
    4 EMA200 pullback continuation A/B LONG if htf_close{-1} > htf_ema_200{-1} and low{-1} <= ema_20{-1} and close{-1} > ema_20{-1} and rsi_14{-1} > 50; SHORT inverse PB Native with MTF M, W
    5 Supertrend flip B LONG if cross_up(close, supertrend_line) and supertrend_dir{-1} == 1; SHORT inverse TR Native if feature exists X
    6 ADX + DI directional surge B LONG if plus_di_14{-1} > minus_di_14{-1} and adx_14{-1} > 25 and adx_14{-1} > adx_14{-5}; SHORT inverse TR Native W
    7 Donchian 20 breakout A/B LONG if close{-1} > highest(high{-20:-2}); SHORT if close{-1} < lowest(low{-20:-2}); else NONE BO Native W
    8 Turtle 55/20 breakout-exit A/B LONG if close{-1} > highest(high{-55:-2}); SHORT if close{-1} < lowest(low{-55:-2}); else NONE TR Native W, O
    9 Bollinger squeeze breakout B LONG if bb_width_pct{-1} < percentile(bb_width_pct{-252:-2},10) and close{-1} > bb_upper{-1}; SHORT if squeeze and close{-1} < bb_lower{-1} BO Native W
    10 Bollinger inside Keltner squeeze release B LONG if squeeze_on{-2} == 1 and squeeze_on{-1} == 0 and momentum_hist{-1} > 0; SHORT if release and momentum_hist{-1} < 0 BO Native if squeeze feature exists signal, W
    11 Aroon trend emergence B LONG if aroon_up_25{-1} > 70 and aroon_down_25{-1} < 30 and aroon_up_25{-1} > aroon_up_25{-5}; SHORT inverse TR Native W
    12 Ichimoku cloud breakout B LONG if close{-1} > ichimoku_cloud_top{-1} and tenkan{-1} > kijun{-1} and chikou_confirm{-1} == 1; SHORT inverse TR Native if features exist signal, M
    13 Linear regression slope breakout B LONG if slope(linreg_close_50{-10:-1}) > 0 and close{-1} > linreg_upper_50{-1}; SHORT inverse BO Native W

    Momentum and relative-strength systems

    Momentum splits naturally into absolute momentum, time-series momentum, cross-sectional or relative momentum, and hybrid forms like dual momentum. The strongest research-backed pieces here are classic momentum and dual momentum. Relative-strength filters and context-symbol confirmation are also among the best reasons to support multi-symbol features in your rule layer. citeturn4search6turn4search10turn4search11turn0search3turn4search1

    ID Strategy Evidence Model rule pseudocode Bot profile Fit Primitive stress
    14 Time-series momentum A LONG if ret_63{-1} > 0 and ret_21{-1} > 0; SHORT if ret_63{-1} < 0 and ret_21{-1} < 0; else NONE TR Native W
    15 Multi-horizon absolute momentum A/B LONG if ret_21{-1} > 0 and ret_63{-1} > 0 and ret_126{-1} > 0; SHORT if all three < 0; else NONE TR Native W
    16 Dual momentum A LONG if ret_63{-1} > 0 and ret_63{-1} > ctx_ret_63{-1}; SHORT if ret_63{-1} < 0 and ret_63{-1} < ctx_ret_63{-1}; else NONE TR Native with context symbol S, W
    17 Relative-strength leader confirmation A/B LONG if rel_strength_vs_ctx{-1} > rel_strength_vs_ctx{-20} and close{-1} > ema_50{-1}; SHORT if relative strength deteriorates and price below ema_50 PB Native with context symbol S, W
    18 ROC acceleration breakout B LONG if roc_20{-1} > roc_20{-5} and roc_20{-1} > 0 and close{-1} > highest(high{-10:-2}); SHORT inverse BO Native W
    19 PPO zero-line momentum B LONG if cross_up(ppo_line, 0) and ppo_line{-1} > ppo_signal{-1}; SHORT if cross_down(ppo_line, 0) and ppo_line{-1} < ppo_signal{-1} TR Native X
    20 TRIX trend entry B LONG if cross_up(trix, trix_signal) and trix{-1} > 0; SHORT if cross_down(...) and trix{-1} < 0 TR Native X
    21 OBV breakout confirmation B LONG if close{-1} > highest(high{-20:-2}) and obv{-1} > highest(obv{-20:-2}); SHORT if price breakdown and obv breaks down too BO Native W
    22 MFI momentum continuation B LONG if mfi_14{-1} > 60 and mfi_14{-1} > mfi_14{-5} and close{-1} > ema_20{-1}; SHORT if mfi < 40 and falling with price below ema_20 PB Native W
    23 Volume impulse breakout B LONG if close{-1} > highest(high{-15:-2}) and volume{-1} > 1.8 * avg(volume{-20:-2}); SHORT inverse BO Native W
    24 VWAP intraday continuation B LONG if session_close{-1} > session_vwap{-1} and pullback_low{-1} <= session_vwap{-1} and bounce_confirm{-1} == 1; SHORT inverse IN Native with session features session, W
    25 Multi-timeframe momentum stack A/B LONG if htf_ret_63{-1} > 0 and mtf_ret_21{-1} > 0 and ltf_roc_5{-1} > 0; SHORT if all three align negative TR Native with MTF M, W
    26 Context-symbol risk-on confirmation B LONG if base_signal_trend{-1} == 1 and ctx_market_risk_on{-1} == 1 and ctx_vol_regime_bad{-1} == 0; SHORT if base bearish and ctx risk-off TR Native with context symbol/regime S, G

    Mean-reversion and range systems

    Mean reversion is much more regime-sensitive than trend following, but it is highly expressible in a rule engine and often benefits most from clean bot exits. Bollinger-based reversion, z-score reversion, and pairs-style spread reversion are especially natural fits for deterministic rules. Gatev, Goetzmann, and Rouwenhorst give the classic academic pairs framework; John Bollinger’s own materials emphasize that the bands answer whether price is relatively high or low, not just whether a breakout occurred. citeturn4search0turn4search4turn4search18turn5search0turn5search3

    Volatility, structure, failure, and hybrid systems

    This last bucket is where your future rule engine earns its keep. These are the strategies that force richer windows, disjoint conditions, precomputed structure features, and more capable bot rules. They are also the ones most likely to reveal whether you need count, bars_since, range functions, trap detection, and order-edit actions. Pairs trading is the clearest example that may push beyond simple single-symbol execution, while hybrid regime-switching is the clearest example that may push beyond plain first-match rule evaluation. citeturn4search0turn4search18turn3search5turn3search8turn3search6

    The table above contains 51 rows because I deliberately split out pair-spread z-score reversion and regime-switch hybrid as distinct must-have strategy archetypes. If you need the list to remain exactly at 50, merge Strategy 15 into Strategy 14 by treating multi-horizon absolute momentum as a parameterized variant of time-series momentum. I would personally keep all 51 because they are materially different strategy classes.

    What these strategies demand from the engine

    The catalog makes the engine requirements very concrete.

    The first must-have block is temporal selection. You need single offsets, continuous ranges, rolling statistics, extrema, count, any, all, bars_since, slopes, z-scores, and percentile-style comparisons. LEAN’s rolling-window model and TradingView’s strategy logic both demonstrate how central trailing windows and deterministic bar-by-bar evaluation are in real strategy implementation. citeturn3search4turn3search5turn3search9

    The second must-have block is bot-side state and action editing. It is not enough to return LONG, SHORT, or NONE. The bot layer needs to support at least OPEN, ADD, REDUCE, CLOSE, REVERSE, SET_SL, UPDATE_SL, SET_TP, UPDATE_TP, ENABLE_TRAIL, UPDATE_TRAIL, MOVE_TO_BREAKEVEN, and FLAT_AT_TIME. That matches what serious strategy platforms already expose in one way or another: TradingView supports stop, profit, and trailing exits; LEAN explicitly supports order-ticket updates and crypto stop replacements; MQL5 has trailing and reverse methods; Backtrader supports signal operation, order creation, stop, and stop-trail workflows. citeturn3search5turn3search8turn3search2turn3search6turn3search3turn0search5

    The third block is feature breadth. A modern feature layer should expose canonical trend, momentum, mean-reversion, volatility, volume, and structure features, plus derived signals such as squeezes, fractals, pivots, pullback flags, breakout flags, and regime labels. TA-Lib’s breadth is a useful reference point for how much indicator variety systematic engines commonly rely on. citeturn5search1turn5search4

    The fourth block is multi-timeframe and multi-symbol support. Strategies 4, 16, 17, 24, 25, 26, 48, and 50 are not fringe. They are mainstream systematic ideas. That means your rule engine should be able to evaluate a base symbol with higher-timeframe context and other-symbol context without leaking future data. The warning from mature systems about repainting and correct bar semantics matters here: completed-bar logic must remain strict. citeturn3search17turn3search1turn3search4

    The only clearly non-trivial outlier in this catalog is coordinated two-leg execution for pairs and spread strategies. Strategy 50 is still worth keeping in the catalog, because it tells you exactly what extra capability would be required: synchronized long-short legs, shared capital accounting, spread state, and spread exits. If you do not want to implement that yet, it becomes a deliberate deferred class rather than an accidental blind spot. The other major potential extension is rule grouping or hierarchical evaluation for Strategy 51, where regime selection routes into a different sub-policy; that is still much smaller than a full platform redesign. citeturn4search0turn4search18turn3search6

    Prioritization

    If the goal is to maximize learning and give Rainbow the best shot at finding actual tradable edges quickly, I would implement the first wave in this order: Donchian breakout, Turtle breakout, EMA200 pullback continuation, ADX + DI trend surge, Bollinger squeeze breakout, time-series momentum, dual momentum, relative-strength confirmation, RSI(2) dip buy in uptrend, Bollinger touch and re-entry, z-score mean reversion, failed breakout reversal, NR7 breakout, VWAP intraday continuation, and regime-switch hybrid. That mix gives you strong coverage across the best-evidenced families, exposes the key rule primitives, and forces the bot to support real exits rather than toy close-on-opposite-signal behavior. Trend following and momentum are the strongest evidence bucket; pairs and regime-switching are the strongest architectural stress tests; VWAP/session logic is the strongest bot-state stress test. citeturn4search1turn4search5turn0search3turn4search6turn4search11turn4search0turn5search5

    The practical message is simple: you do not need to guess what kinds of rules the future engine should support. These strategies already tell you. If the engine can express these model rules and the bot can execute these management profiles, Rainbow will be able to cover most of the classic deterministic strategy space that is actually worth researching.
